items.stem: Which practice misleads a viewer about the size of differences between bars?

options.text: Truncating the value axis so it does not start at zero
options.rationale: Correct: a non-zero baseline on a bar chart visually exaggerates differences.
Sorting bars aids comparison and does not mislead.

options.text: Labeling each bar with its value
options.rationale: Direct labels add precision, not distortion.
A consistent color is a neutral, honest choice.

items.explanation: Correct: a non-zero baseline on a bar chart visually exaggerates differences.

items.stem: A pre-attentive attribute such as color is useful in a chart because it...

options.text: Draws the eye to the most important element almost instantly
options.rationale: Correct: pre-attentive attributes are noticed almost instantly, guiding attention.

options.text: Guarantees the chart is accessible to everyone
options.rationale: Color alone does not guarantee accessibility; contrast and redundancy matter.

options.text: Replaces the need for any labels
options.rationale: Labels are still needed for precise reading.

options.text: Always makes a chart more precise
options.rationale: Color draws attention but does not inherently add precision.

items.stem: Which TWO improve the clarity and integrity of a chart? (Select TWO)

options.text: Removing non-data ink such as heavy gridlines and borders
options.rationale: Correct: removing chart junk focuses attention on the data.

options.text: Starting a bar chart's value axis at zero
options.rationale: Correct: a zero baseline on bars represents magnitudes honestly.
3D effects distort perception and add no information.

options.text: Using many bright colors for every category
options.rationale: Overusing bright colors creates clutter and reduces clarity.
